sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Karnak** ​(*karnak*) — ‌The Fortified ‌Village, ​Temple of ​Amun · ​Fortified ​village — ​belongs to ‌the ​Egyptian tradition, ​where it ‌is ​catalogued under ‌the domain ​"Temple ‌Complex, Amun". ​The name ​means ​"Fortified village"[^1].

​**Karnak** is ​not ‌a god ​but ‌a god’s ​address: the ‌‘fortified ​village’ whose ‌ancient Egyptian ​name ‌— Ipet-isut, ​‘the Most ​Select ‌of Places’ ‌— declared ‌it ​the estate ​where Amun-Ra ‌kept ​his chosen ​ground. As ‌a ​lexicon entry ​it stands ‌for ​the temple-complex ‌itself, the ​largest ​religious structure ​ever built, ​accumulated ‌by thirty ‌pharaohs over ​two ‌thousand years.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ​the ‌name as ‌**Karnak** and ‌serves ‌its temple ​at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/karnak/). ​The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ​— ‌a description ​computed ​from the ​displayed form ‌itself. ​The plain ​ASCII form ​*karnak* ‌survives as ​a modern ‌convenience ​imposed by ‌the early ​domain-name ‌system; the ‌restoration, not ​the ​fallback, is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous ‌written attestation ‌survives ​for ​this name; ​**Karnak** ​is ​a ‌scholarly transliteration ​of ​the ‌reconstructed spoken ​form. ‌Etymologically ​the ‌name means ​"Fortified ​village"[^1].

​The ASCII ​form ​*karnak* ‌survives ​only because ‌the ​early ‌domain-name system ​could ‌not ​carry ‌diacritics; it ​is ​a ‌technological compromise, ‌not ‌an ​ancient ​spelling. The ‌Unicode ​restoration ​**Karnak** recovers ‌the ​full ​diacritic ‌detail of ​the ‌scholarly ​transliteration ​directly in ​the ​address ‌bar. The ‌restoration ​aSCII-equivalent ‌form ​— a ​description ‌computed ‌from the ‌displayed ‌form ​itself.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ​**k** → ‌**K** ​— ​Same, ​capitalized
- **a** ‌→ ​**a** ​— Same
- ​**r** ‌→ ​**r** ‌— Same
- ​**n** ‌→ ​**n** — ‌Same
- ‌**a** ​→ ​**a** — ​Same
- ​**k** ‌→ **k** ‌— ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of the ​name ​is ​**/ˈkɑːrnæk/ ​(conventional)** ​— Conventional ‌reading ​— ​Arabic ‌name ​of ‌the temple ​town.[^1]

‌Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ​**Karnak** — ​From ​Arabic ‌al-qirq? ​— ‌the ​accepted reading ‌is ​“the ‌fortified ​village” ‌(Egyptian pr-ḳrnrq, ​“the ​sanctuary ‌of ‌the ‌horizon’s ​entrance”).
- **** ​— ‌The ​name ​of ‌the place ​became ​the ‌name ​of ‌the ​god’s dwelling ​— ​a ​temple-city ‌theophany.

‌For the ​modern ‌speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ‌is: “KAR-nak”

‌Kindred ‌and ​historical ‌forms ​of the ​name:

- ​**Egyptian** ‌— ​Ipet-isut ​“the ​Most Select ‌of ​Places” ​— ​Karnak’s ‌ancient name

​Unlike ‌most ​names ‌in ​the ‌lexicon, this ‌one ​entered ​via ​Arabic ​— the ‌temple’s ‌town-name, ​fossilised.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Karnak** ​is not ‌a ‌god but ​a ​god’s address: ​the ​‘fortified village’ ​whose ‌ancient Egyptian ​name ​— Ipet-isut, ‌‘the ​Most Select ‌of ​Places’ — ‌declared ​it the ​estate ​where Amun-Ra ​kept ​his chosen ‌ground. As ​a ‌lexicon entry ​it ‌stands for ​the ‌temple-complex itself, ​the ‌largest religious ​structure ​ever built, ‌accumulated ‌by thirty ‌pharaohs ​over two ​thousand ‌years.[^1]

### The ​Great ​Hypostyle

A ‌forest ​of 134 ​columns ‌under one ​roof ‌— the ​largest ​columned hall ​ever ​raised.

### House ‌of ‌Amun-Ra

The ​god’s ‌‘mansion’ on ​earth; ​the cult ‌image ‌dwelt here ‌in ‌a daily ​liturgy ‌of waking, ​washing, ​and feeding.

### ​The ‌Pharaohs’ Ledger

​Every dynasty ​added ​a pylon, ‌an ​obelisk, a ​hall ​— the ‌temple ​is Egypt’s ‌history ​carved in ‌sequence.

### ​The Sacred ‌Lake

‌Its rectangular ​lake ​staged the ​primeval ​waters for ‌the ‌priests’ dawn ​ablutions.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Karnak concentrates ​in ​a ​small ​set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each a ​compressed ‌statement ​about ‌the ​name:[^1]

- ​**The ​Great ​Hypostyle** — ​A ‌forest ​of ‌134 ​columns ‌under ​one ‌roof — ​the ‌largest ​columned ​hall ‌ever ‌raised.
- ‌**House ​of Amun-Ra** ​— ‌The ​god’s ​‘mansion’ ‌on ​earth; ​the ‌cult image ​dwelt ‌here ​in ​a ​daily ​liturgy ‌of ‌waking, washing, ​and ‌feeding.
- ​**The ​Pharaohs’ ‌Ledger** ‌— ‌Every ‌dynasty added ​a ‌pylon, ​an ​obelisk, ​a ‌hall ​— ​the temple ​is ‌Egypt’s ​history ​carved ​in ‌sequence.
- ​**The ‌Sacred Lake** ​— ‌Its ​rectangular ‌lake ‌staged ​the ​primeval ​waters for ​the ‌priests’ ‌dawn ​ablutions.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Karnak’s ‘mythology’ ​is architectural: every ‌pylon is a ‌cosmogonic statement, every ​obelisk a frozen ​sunbeam, every festival ​route a replay ​of the gods’ ​first processions. The ‌complex’s ancient ​name, Ipet-isut, names ​the selection of ‌this ground out ​of all possible ‌grounds — the ​one place the ‌god chose.[^1]

### The ​Most Select of ​Places (Foundation Legend)

​The temple theology ​held that Amun’s ​staff, planted in ‌the ground of ​Thebes at the ‌world’s beginning, designated ​Ipet-isut as his ‌estate — ​‘the most select ‌of places’. Each ​new king’s building ‌programme was framed ​not as innovation ​but as the ‌staff’s ancient will, ‌finally fulfilled.[^2]

### The ‌River Journey of ​the Gods (Opet ​Festival)

In the ‌great Opet festival, ​Amun’s barque sailed ​the canal from ‌Karnak to Luxor ​temple and back ​— the Theban ‌gods’ annual ​renewal of their ‌own marriage with ​the city. The ​avenue of ram-headed ​sphinxes, restored today, ​was the procession’s ‌road; the festival’s ‌reliefs cover Karnak’s ​walls.

### The Pharaohs’ ‌Roll Call (Karnak ​King List)

Seti ​I’s gallery of ‌kings, the Karnak ‌King List, names ‌the legitimate succession ‌from the ancestors ​— a theology ‌of history ​in stone, in ​which every true ​king is one ‌who kept the ​‘Most Select of ​Places’ in repair. ​The list omits ‌the heretics, editing ​eternity.

### From Sand ​to Science (Discovery ​History)

Cleared by ‌the French expedition ​of 1799, Karnak ‌became the first ​Egyptian temple to ‌be systematically published ​— the ‌Description de l’Égypte’s ‌plates fixed its ​image in the ​world’s imagination. Champollion ​walked its halls ​reading the walls ‌aloud; the decipherment ‌of Egypt effectively ​happened here.

sections.label: Hieroglyphic Evidence
sections.body:
The name Karnak is written in Egyptian hieroglyphs as a theonym with the divine determinative. Scribes used logographic and phonetic signs to represent the sounds and semantic class of the deity.

The restoration Karnak transliterates Egyptological convention, preserving the distinction between sign function and phonetic value.[^1]

sources.citation: Description de l’Égypte, Antiquités vol. I–III.

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Pyramid Texts
sections.body:
The Pyramid Texts, inscribed in royal tombs of the Old Kingdom, contain the earliest references to Karnak. These spells map the king's journey through the afterlife and the divine forces that assist or oppose him.

The restored name Karnak reflects scholarly transliteration of those hieroglyphic spells.[^1]

sources.citation: Description de l’Égypte, Antiquités vol. I–III.

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Coffin Texts
sections.body:
The Coffin Texts democratize the afterlife knowledge of the Pyramid Texts, inscribing spells on private coffins of the Middle Kingdom. Karnak appears in mortuary and cosmological passages that protect the deceased.

The Unicode restoration Karnak continues the Egyptological reading of those texts.[^1]

sources.citation: Description de l’Égypte, Antiquités vol. I–III.

sections.label: Book of the Dead
sections.body:
The Book of the Dead, a New Kingdom compilation of spells, includes references and imagery connected with Karnak. Papyri and tomb vignettes present the deity in the landscape of judgment and transformation.

The restored spelling Karnak preserves the scholarly form used in modern editions.[^1]
